title: Selecting HTML Elements with Javascript
summary: Covers the five DOM selection methods: getElementsByTagName, getElementsByClassName, getElementById, querySelector and querySelectorAll. Explains single-element vs collection return values, CSS-selector syntax inside querySelector, and finishes with a challenge to colour a nested link red.

concepts.heading: getElementsByTagName
points: Takes a tag name string such as "li" and returns every matching element on the page, as an array-like collection. Plural 'Elements' in the name signals a collection.
Each item is a full element object with properties to read or set.

You cannot set style on the collection itself: document.getElementsByTagName('li').style.color fails with a misleading 'cannot set property of undefined' style error, because a collection has no style. Pick one element with square brackets first, e.g. [2] for the third item (indexes start at 0).
Because it is array-like, .length gives the number of matches (3 li items on the demo page).

concepts.heading: getElementsByClassName
points: Takes a class name (no dot) and also returns a collection, even if only one element has the class. The button with class btn still needs [0].
Use the index before setting properties, e.g. getElementsByClassName('btn')[0].style.color = 'red'.

concepts.heading: getElementById
points: Singular 'Element': returns one element, not a collection, because an id should be unique per page. Takes the id with no # sign.
Direct property use works: document.getElementById('title').innerHTML = 'Good Bye' changes the h1's text.

concepts.heading: querySelector
points: Accepts any CSS selector string and returns a single element: the first match in document order.
Selector syntax is identical to CSS: bare name for tag, dot prefix for class, # prefix for id.
Descendant selector uses a space: 'li a' picks the anchor inside a li, not a free-standing a elsewhere. Plain 'a' would return the first anchor in the document.
Compound selector without a space: 'li.item' is an li that also has class item (same element). '#list a' is an anchor anywhere under the element with id list.
If several elements match (e.g. '#list .item' matches three li), only the first is returned.

concepts.heading: querySelectorAll
points: Same selector argument, but returns all matches as a collection (a NodeList). Pick elements with an index, e.g. [2].
(Extra) NodeList also has forEach and length, but it is not a real array; getElementsBy... returns a live HTMLCollection.

concepts.heading: Which to use
points: querySelector / querySelectorAll are more flexible: any combination of tag, class, id and nesting can be expressed, so they are the ones commonly seen in real code.
The getElement... methods are more limited and make it harder to target one specific element without editing the HTML.
Try all of them to see which fits best.

task.name: Colour the nested Google link red
task.starting_point: The demo page, which has one free-standing link and another inside the first li.
task.goal: Turn the text of the link that is inside the list item red, not the other link.
steps: Open the console on the page.
Inspect the DOM tree: the link is an anchor inside an li.
Select it with a descendant selector, e.g. querySelector('li a').
Confirm the highlighted element is the right one.
task.expected_result: The Google link inside the list is red; the free-standing link is unchanged.
task.reference_repo_path: Section 16 - The Document Object Model (DOM)/16.03 - Selecting HTML Elements with Javascript/script.js

pitfalls: Forgetting the index on a collection, then trying to set .style on it.
Using # or . inside getElementById / getElementsByClassName (they take bare names).
Selecting the li instead of the nested a: colouring the li only changes the bullet marker because the link is a separate element with its own colour.
Expecting querySelector to return every match.
Space vs no space in selectors: 'li a' (descendant) and 'li.item' (same element) mean different things.
